Shave
SHAYV
v.t.
From Anglo-Saxon scafan, to scrape or pare. Webster 1828: to cut or pare off something from the surface by a razor. In Scripture shaving is almost always ritual or judicial — a sign of cleansing, of mourning, of humiliation, or of a vow interrupted.

Biblical Definition

Shaving in Israel was rarely cosmetic. The Nazarite whose vow was defiled by a sudden death must begin again, and the razor marks the interruption: he hath defiled the head of his consecration; then he shall shave his head in the day of his cleansing, on the seventh day shall he shave it (Numbers 6:9). The cleansed leper shaves; so does the captive woman a man would marry, whose old life is deliberately put off: thou shalt bring her home to thine house; and she shall shave her head, and pare her nails (Deuteronomy 21:12) — a law which, whatever else it does, forbids the treatment of a captive as spoil and requires a full month before marriage. Isaiah turns shaving into a figure of national humiliation with a razor God has hired: In the same day shall the Lord shave with a razor that is hired, namely, by them beyond the river, by the king of Assyria, the head, and the hair of the feet: and it shall also consume the beard (Isaiah 7:20). Paul appeals to the same sense of disgrace in his argument about covering: if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered (1 Corinthians 11:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SHAVE as to cut or pare off something from the surface of a body by a razor or other edged instrument; to cut off the hair from the skin.

SHAVE, v.t. — To cut or pare off something from the surface of a body by a razor or other edged instrument.

To cut off the hair from the skin with a razor; as, to shave the head.

To skim along the surface near to; to sweep along.

To strip; to oppress by extortion; to fleece.

Anglo-Saxon scafan, to scrape or shave; compare shape and scab.

Key Scripture

Numbers 6:9 — "And if any man die very suddenly by him, and he hath defiled the head of his consecration; then he shall shave his head in the day of his cleansing, on the seventh day shall he shave it."

Deuteronomy 21:12 — "Then thou shalt bring her home to thine house; and she shall shave her head, and pare her nails;"

Isaiah 7:20 — "In the same day shall the Lord shave with a razor that is hired, namely, by them beyond the river, by the king of Assyria, the head, and the hair of the feet: and it shall also consume the beard."

1 Corinthians 11:6 — "For if the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn: but if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered."

Modern Corruption

Deuteronomy 21:10-14 is regularly cited as evidence that Scripture licenses the taking of captive women, when the law it states is a restraint that forbids exactly that treatment.

expand to see more

The passage is a favourite of the popular case against the Old Testament, and its actual provisions run the other way. A captive woman may not be used; she is brought into the house, her head shaved and nails pared, her captive’s clothing removed, and she bewails her father and mother a full month — and only then may she be married, as a wife with a wife’s standing. If the man has no delight in her she must be let go free, and the law states the reason plainly: thou shalt not sell her at all for money, thou shalt not make merchandise of her, because thou hast humbled her (Deuteronomy 21:14). In an ancient world where captive women were property, this legislation interposes a month of mourning, a formal marriage, and a prohibition on sale. The Mosaic case laws regulate a fallen world without endorsing it, and reading a restraint as a permission inverts the text.

1 Corinthians 11:6 rests on a cultural fact — that a shorn or shaven head was a disgrace to a woman in Corinth — and builds on a creational argument that is not cultural: the order of headship in verse 3, which runs God, Christ, man, woman, and which Paul grounds in the account of creation. Two errors follow from missing the distinction. The first treats the whole passage as time-bound and discards the order along with the head-covering; the second absolutizes the local sign and makes a first-century Corinthian custom a permanent ordinance. This dictionary holds the creational order that Paul argues from, while recognising that the sign by which it was expressed in Corinth was a sign, and that Paul himself ends the passage by appealing to the custom of the churches.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew galach (H1548), to shave or make bald; taar (H8593), a razor; Greek xurao (G3587), to shave; keiro (G2751), to shear.

expand to see more

Hebrew galach (H1548) — to shave, to make bald; used of the Nazarite (Numbers 6:9) and the captive woman (Deuteronomy 21:12).

Hebrew taar (H8593) — a razor; the hired razor of Isaiah 7:20, which is Assyria.

Greek xurao (G3587) — to shave with a razor; shorn or shaven (1 Corinthians 11:6).

Greek keiro (G2751) — to shear or cut short, as a sheep; the companion verb in the same verse.

Hebrew nezer (H5145) — consecration, separation; the head of his consecration (Numbers 6:9).

Usage

"He shall shave his head in the day of his cleansing (Numbers 6:9) — a vow defiled must begin again."

"She shall shave her head, and pare her nails (Deuteronomy 21:12) — a law of restraint, not of licence."

"The Lord shall shave with a razor that is hired (Isaiah 7:20) — Assyria as God’s hired instrument of humiliation."
